sections.title: Vertices, Edges, and Two Ways to Write Them Down
sections.body:
A **simple graph** is a pair $G = (V, E)$ where $V$ is a finite set of **vertices** and $E$ is a set of **edges**, each edge an unordered pair $\{u, v\}$ of distinct vertices. *Simple* is doing real work here: no edge from a vertex to itself, and no pair listed twice, so $E \subseteq \{\, \{u,v\} : u, v \in V,\ u \neq v \,\}$.

Two vertices joined by an edge are **adjacent**, and that edge is **incident** to both of them. On a computer a graph is stored either as an **adjacency matrix** - an $n \times n$ array with $A_{ij} = 1$ exactly when $\{i,j\} \in E$ - or as an **adjacency list**, one list of neighbours per vertex.

For a simple graph the matrix is always symmetric with a zero diagonal, and it costs $n^2$ entries whatever $|E|$ is, while the lists cost $2|E|$ because each edge appears once from each end.
sections.code:
G = (V, E)
V = {a, b, c, d, e}
E = { {a,b}, {a,c}, {b,c}, {c,d}, {d,e} }        |V| = 5,   |E| = 5

Adjacency matrix A   (rows and columns in the order a b c d e)

        a  b  c  d  e
   a  [ 0  1  1  0  0 ]
   b  [ 1  0  1  0  0 ]
   c  [ 1  1  0  1  0 ]
   d  [ 0  0  1  0  1 ]
   e  [ 0  0  0  1  0 ]

Adjacency list
   a -> b, c
   b -> a, c
   c -> a, b, d
   d -> c, e
   e -> d

A is symmetric: A[i][j] = A[j][i], because {u,v} and {v,u} are one edge.
Its diagonal is all 0: no vertex is joined to itself.
Storage: the matrix always uses 5 x 5 = 25 entries;
the list stores each edge twice, 2|E| = 10 endpoints in total.

annotations.text: Edges are unordered pairs, so $\{a,b\}$ and $\{b,a\}$ name the same single edge.
Row $c$ has three 1s: $c$ is adjacent to $a$, $b$ and $d$. A row sum is a degree.
Symmetry is forced by the edges being unordered - it is not a storage convention.
The matrix does not care how sparse $G$ is; the list does. That is the whole trade.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the adjacency matrix and the adjacency list for the simple graph $K = (\{1,2,3,4\},\ \{\,\{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\}, \{3,4\}\,\})$. Rows and columns are in the order $1,2,3,4$.
checkpoint.template:
row 1:  0 1 1 0
row 2:  1 0 ___ 0
row 3:  1 1 0 ___
row 4:  0 0 1 ___

neighbours of 3:  1, 2, ___
number of entries in the full 4x4 matrix:  ___
checkpoint.explain: The entry $A_{44}$ is on the diagonal and a simple graph has no loop at a vertex, so it is $0$, while $A_{23} = A_{32} = 1$ because one undirected edge appears on both sides of the diagonal. The matrix holds $4^2 = 16$ entries no matter that only $4$ edges exist - sparsity buys nothing in this representation.

sections.title: Degree and the Handshake Lemma
sections.body:
The **degree** $\deg(v)$ of a vertex is the number of edges incident to it, which in a simple graph is just its number of neighbours. The **handshake lemma** says that for every graph

$$\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2|E|.$$

The proof is **double counting**: count the pairs (vertex, edge it lies on) by vertex and you get $\sum_{v} \deg(v)$; count the same pairs by edge and you get $2$ per edge, because every edge has exactly two endpoints.

Two consequences do most of the work in practice. The degree sum is always **even**, so the number of vertices of odd degree is even; and if $G$ is $k$-**regular** - every vertex of degree $k$ - then $|E| = \frac{kn}{2}$, which forces $kn$ to be even.
sections.code:
Degrees in the same G

   deg(a) = 2      neighbours b, c
   deg(b) = 2      neighbours a, c
   deg(c) = 3      neighbours a, b, d
   deg(d) = 2      neighbours c, e
   deg(e) = 1      neighbour  d
   -------------------------------------------------
   sum      = 10   =  2 x 5  =  2|E|      (handshake lemma)

Why it is true - count one set of things in two ways.
Let P = { (v, e) : v is a vertex, e is an edge, v is an endpoint of e }.

   count P by vertex:   each v appears in deg(v) pairs   ->  sum of deg(v)
   count P by edge:     each e has exactly 2 endpoints   ->  2|E|

Corollary: 5 vertices each of degree 3 would give sum = 15, which is odd.
Then 2|E| = 15 and |E| = 7.5. Impossible - no such graph exists.

annotations.text: $c$ and $e$ are the odd-degree vertices, and there are exactly two of them - never an odd number.
$10 = 2 \times 5$. The check costs nothing and catches most edge-list mistakes.
Naming the set you are counting is what turns a double-counting argument into a proof.
Parity alone rules the graph out. You never have to search for it.

checkpoint.prompt: A simple graph has $7$ vertices and every vertex has degree $4$. How many edges does it have? Show the handshake step, and say what would go wrong if the degree were $3$ instead.
checkpoint.explain: The degree sum is $7 \times 4 = 28$, so $|E| = 28/2 = 14$. With degree $3$ the sum would be $21$, an odd number, and $2|E|$ is even for every graph - so a $3$-regular graph on $7$ vertices cannot exist at all. Parity of the degree sum is a feasibility test you can run before drawing anything.

sections.title: Walks, Paths, Cycles, Connectivity
sections.body:
A **walk** is a sequence of vertices in which each consecutive pair is joined by an edge; its **length** is the number of edges used, and nothing stops it revisiting a vertex. A **path** is a walk in which no vertex repeats, and a **cycle** is a walk of length at least $3$ that starts and ends at the same vertex and otherwise repeats nothing.

If there is any walk from $u$ to $v$, there is a path: keep cutting out the stretch between two visits to a repeated vertex and the walk gets strictly shorter, so a shortest $u$-$v$ walk cannot repeat a vertex at all.

$G$ is **connected** when every pair of vertices has a path between them. In general $V$ splits into **connected components** - maximal sets of mutually reachable vertices - and a graph with more than one component contains pairs with no walk between them whatsoever.
sections.code:
Sequences in G = ({a,b,c,d,e}, { ab, ac, bc, cd, de })

   a-b-c-d-e     walk yes,  path yes    no vertex repeats
   a-b-c-a-b     walk yes,  path no     a and b repeat
   a-b-c-a       closed walk, and a cycle of length 3
   a-c-b-a       the same cycle, read the other way round

Connectivity of H = ({1,...,7}, { 12, 13, 23, 45, 56, 67 })

   start at 1:  reach 2, 3                  component {1, 2, 3}
   start at 4:  reach 5, then 6, then 7     component {4, 5, 6, 7}

   2 components, so H is not connected.
   Note 1 and 4 have no walk between them at all.

annotations.text: A walk may repeat as much as it likes. That freedom is why walks are easy to build and paths are the useful ones.
A cycle is a subgraph, not a starting point: $a$-$b$-$c$-$a$ and $a$-$c$-$b$-$a$ are one cycle of length 3.
Reachability is an equivalence relation on $V$, and its classes are exactly the components.
Connectivity is a property of the whole graph, decided by searching from each unvisited vertex.

checkpoint.prompt: Using $G = (\{a,b,c,d,e\},\ \{ab, ac, bc, cd, de\})$ from the worked example, classify each sequence with the most specific label that applies: `walk`, `path` or `cycle`.
checkpoint.template:
a-c-d-e        is a ___
b-c-b-a        is a ___ but not a path
b-c-a-b        is a ___
number of connected components of G:  ___
checkpoint.explain: `b-c-b-a` reuses the edge $bc$ and revisits $b$, so it is only a walk, while `b-c-a-b` returns to its start with nothing else repeated, which makes it a cycle of length $3$. Every vertex of $G$ is reachable from every other, so $G$ has a single component and is connected.

sections.title: Trees, and Two Colours
sections.body:
A **tree** is a graph that is **connected** and **acyclic**, and a **leaf** is a vertex of degree $1$. Every tree on $n \geq 2$ vertices has a leaf, and deleting a leaf leaves a tree - which gives an induction proving that a tree on $n$ vertices has exactly $n - 1$ edges.

The same argument applied to each component shows that a **forest** - an acyclic graph - with $n$ vertices and $c$ components has exactly $n - c$ edges, so an acyclic graph never has more than $n - 1$ edges.

$G$ is **bipartite** when $V$ splits into two parts $X$ and $Y$ with every edge running between them, equivalently when the vertices can be given two colours so that no edge joins equal colours. Colouring along a cycle alternates, so a bipartite graph has no cycle of odd length, and every tree - having no cycles at all - is bipartite.
sections.code:
A tree is a graph that is connected and acyclic.

   T = ({1,...,6}, { 12, 13, 34, 35, 26 })     |V| = 6,  |E| = 5 = |V| - 1

Induction on n = |V|, claim: every tree on n vertices has n - 1 edges.
   base   n = 1:  one vertex, no edges,  0 = 1 - 1.
   step   a tree on n >= 2 vertices has a leaf v (a vertex of degree 1);
          delete v and its single edge - still connected, still acyclic,
          so it is a tree on n - 1 vertices, with n - 2 edges by hypothesis;
          put v and its edge back:  (n - 2) + 1 = n - 1.

Two-colouring T, starting from vertex 1:
   1:A    2:B    3:B    4:A    5:A    6:A
   every edge joins an A to a B, so T is bipartite,
   with parts X = {1, 4, 5, 6} and Y = {2, 3}.

C5 = 1-2-3-4-5-1 forces the colours A B A B A,
and then the edge {5,1} joins A to A. C5 is not bipartite.

annotations.text: Six vertices, five edges. Add any edge to a tree and you close a cycle; remove any edge and it disconnects.
The leaf is what makes the induction possible - without it there is nothing safe to delete.
One vertex restored, one edge restored, so the claim $n - 1$ survives the step.
An odd cycle is the only obstruction that matters: a graph is bipartite exactly when it has none.

checkpoint.prompt: A tree $T$ has $20$ vertices. How many edges does it have, and what is $\sum_{v} \deg(v)$ for $T$? Then say whether $T$ is bipartite, with a reason.
checkpoint.explain: A tree on $n$ vertices has $n - 1 = 19$ edges, and the handshake lemma turns that straight into a degree sum of $2 \times 19 = 38$. $T$ is bipartite because bipartiteness fails only when an odd cycle exists, and a tree has no cycles of any length.

guided-practice.prompt: Let $H = (\{1,2,3,4\},\ \{\,\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\}\,\})$. Complete the last rows of its adjacency matrix (order $1,2,3,4$) and the degree summary below it.
guided-practice.template:
row 1:  0 1 1 0
row 2:  1 0 1 0
row 3:  1 1 ___ 1
row 4:  0 0 1 ___

deg(3) = ___
sum of all degrees = ___
|E| = ___
guided-practice.explain: Both missing matrix entries are diagonal ones, and a simple graph has no loops, so $A_{33} = A_{44} = 0$. Reading degrees off the row sums gives $2 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 8 = 2|E|$, hence $|E| = 4$ - the edge list you were handed, now recovered from the matrix instead of copied.

guided-practice.prompt: (a) A simple graph is $4$-regular and has $12$ edges. How many vertices does it have? (b) Explain why there is no graph with five vertices each of degree $3$. Use the handshake lemma in both parts and show the arithmetic.
guided-practice.explain: In (a) the degree sum is $2|E| = 24$ and each vertex contributes $4$, so $n = 24/4 = 6$ - and such a graph really does exist, namely $K_6$ with a perfect matching deleted. In (b) the degree sum would be $5 \times 3 = 15$, but $2|E|$ is even for every graph, so parity kills it without any search through candidate graphs.

guided-practice.prompt: For $G = (\{a,b,c,d,e\},\ \{ab,\ ac,\ bc,\ cd,\ de\})$, work out each degree, then the degree sum, then recover $|E|$ from the handshake lemma. Give every answer as a single integer.

steps.label: number of vertices of odd degree

guided-practice.explain: Reading degrees off an edge list is just counting how often each letter appears, and the total number of appearances is $2|E| = 10$ because each edge contributes its two endpoints. The odd-degree vertices are $c$ and $e$ - two of them, and there can never be an odd number, since the odd degrees have to sum to an even total.

guided-practice.prompt: Suppose there is a walk from $u$ to $v$ in a graph. Explain why there must also be a **path** from $u$ to $v$, and why a shortest $u$-$v$ walk can never repeat a vertex.
guided-practice.explain: If a walk visits some vertex $w$ twice, everything strictly between the two visits can be deleted and what remains is still a walk from $u$ to $v$, but strictly shorter. A shortest walk therefore admits no such deletion, so it repeats nothing and is a path - which is why 'joined by a walk' and 'joined by a path' define the same relation on $V$.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill in each count. $K_n$ is the complete simple graph on $n$ vertices, in which every pair of distinct vertices is joined by an edge.
guided-practice.template:
a tree with 12 vertices has ___ edges
a forest with 10 vertices and 3 components has ___ edges
the complete graph K5 has ___ edges
the sum of all degrees in K5 is ___
the number of components of a connected graph is ___
guided-practice.explain: A tree gives $n - 1$ and a forest gives $n - c$, which is the tree count applied once per component. $K_5$ has $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ edges and every vertex has degree $4$, so its degree sum is $5 \times 4 = 40 = 2 \times 10$ - the handshake lemma checking itself.

proof-work.prompt: Prove the handshake lemma: for every simple graph $G = (V, E)$, $$\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2|E|.$$ Argue by counting one set in two ways, and name that set explicitly before you count it.
proof-work.explain: The whole proof lives in the set $P = \{(v, e) : v \in V,\ e \in E,\ v \text{ an endpoint of } e\}$: grouping $P$ by its first coordinate gives $\sum_{v} \deg(v)$, grouping by its second gives $2$ per edge. Because $G$ is simple, every edge has exactly two distinct endpoints, and that is the step making the second count $2|E|$ rather than something looser.

proof-work.prompt: Put these steps in order to prove that in any graph, the number of vertices of odd degree is even.
fragments: So the sum of the odd degrees is even, being an even total minus an even number.
Split $V$ into $A$, the vertices of even degree, and $B$, the vertices of odd degree.
A sum of odd numbers is even exactly when there is an even number of terms, so $|B|$ is even.
By the handshake lemma $\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2|E|$, which is even.
The sum of the degrees over $A$ is even, since every term in it is even.
proof-work.explain: The argument only runs in this direction: the handshake lemma supplies an even total first, and the even-degree part is then subtracted off to isolate the odd part. The last step is the arithmetic fact that odd numbers sum to an even value exactly when you add an even count of them.

proof-work.prompt: Prove by induction on $n$ that every tree on $n$ vertices has exactly $n - 1$ edges. You may use without proof that every tree with $n \geq 2$ vertices has a leaf. State your base case, state your inductive hypothesis, and justify why the graph left after deleting the leaf is still a tree.
proof-work.explain: Deleting a leaf $v$ is safe in both directions: removing a degree-$1$ vertex cannot disconnect anything, because no path between two other vertices ever passes through $v$, and removing edges can never create a cycle. That is what licenses the inductive hypothesis on the smaller tree, and restoring $v$ adds exactly one vertex and one edge, so $(n - 2) + 1 = n - 1$.

proof-work.prompt: Prove that a bipartite graph contains no cycle of odd length. Take $G$ bipartite with parts $X$ and $Y$, and consider an arbitrary cycle $v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_k = v_0$.
proof-work.explain: Every edge crosses between $X$ and $Y$, so the side you stand on flips at each step: taking $v_0 \in X$, the vertex $v_i$ lies in $X$ exactly when $i$ is even. Closing the cycle demands $v_k = v_0 \in X$, which forces $k$ to be even, so no odd cycle can sit inside a bipartite graph - and that single obstruction is why $C_5$ fails to be bipartite.

exam.prompt: Which statement is the definition of a **simple graph**?
choices: A graph in which every vertex has the same degree.
A graph whose edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with no repeated edge and no loop.
A graph that is connected and contains no cycle.
A graph whose vertex set splits into two parts with every edge running between them.
exam.explain: The other three options define regular, tree and bipartite - properties a graph may or may not have - whereas *simple* is a restriction on what $E$ is allowed to contain in the first place. It is what makes $\deg(v)$ equal the neighbour count and the adjacency matrix diagonal all zero.

exam.prompt: Which statement is the definition of a **tree**?
choices: A connected graph with exactly one cycle.
A graph in which every vertex has degree at most $2$.
exam.explain: Both halves are needed: an acyclic graph that is not connected is a forest, and a connected graph carrying a cycle has more than $n - 1$ edges. Drop either half and the edge count $n - 1$ - the property the rest of this floor keeps using - stops being true.

exam.prompt: Fill in the counts. Every graph mentioned is simple.
exam.template:
a graph with degree sequence 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3 has ___ edges
a 3-regular graph with 9 edges has ___ vertices
a tree with 15 vertices has ___ edges
the degree sum of that tree is ___
exam.explain: Each answer is one use of $\sum_{v} \deg(v) = 2|E|$: the sequence sums to $12$ so $|E| = 6$, and a $3$-regular graph with $9$ edges has degree sum $18$ and therefore $18/3 = 6$ vertices. The tree supplies the other identity, $|E| = n - 1 = 14$, which the handshake lemma converts into a degree sum of $28$.

exam.prompt: Order these steps into a correct proof that no simple graph has five vertices each of degree $3$.
fragments: But $|E|$ counts edges, so it must be an integer - contradiction.
Suppose for contradiction that such a graph $G = (V, E)$ exists.
exam.explain: The contradiction has to be set up before the arithmetic is done, and the handshake lemma can only be applied once the degree sum has actually been computed. What kills the graph is parity: an odd degree sum can never equal $2|E|$.

exam.prompt: Two-colour $C_6$, the cycle $1-2-3-4-5-6-1$, giving vertex $1$ the colour $A$ and colouring each new vertex the opposite colour to the neighbour you reached it from, walking $1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4 \to 5 \to 6$. Answer the colour steps with `A` or `B` and the last three with `yes` or `no`.

steps.label: does the edge {6,1} join two equal colours?
would C6 with the extra edge {1,3} still be bipartite?

exam.explain: Colours alternate along the cycle, so vertex $i$ receives $A$ exactly when $i$ is odd; the closing edge $\{6,1\}$ joins $B$ to $A$, and an even cycle always closes consistently like this. Adding $\{1,3\}$ creates the triangle $1-2-3-1$, an odd cycle, and by the odd-cycle obstruction no two-colouring can survive it.

exam.prompt: Explain why the adjacency matrix of a simple graph is symmetric and has a zero diagonal, and state what each of those two properties says about $E$.
exam.explain: Symmetry restates that edges are unordered pairs: $\{u,v\}$ and $\{v,u\}$ are the same element of $E$, so $A_{uv}$ and $A_{vu}$ must agree. The zero diagonal restates that the two endpoints are distinct, i.e. no loops - both are consequences of the definition of *simple*, not conventions you could choose otherwise.

exam.prompt: A tree $T$ has exactly three vertices of degree $4$, exactly two vertices of degree $3$, and every remaining vertex is a leaf. How many vertices does $T$ have in total? Show your working.
exam.explain: Writing $L$ for the number of leaves gives $n = 5 + L$ and a degree sum of $3(4) + 2(3) + L = 18 + L$, while the handshake lemma together with $|E| = n - 1$ forces that same sum to be $2(n - 1) = 8 + 2L$. Solving $18 + L = 8 + 2L$ gives $L = 10$ and $n = 15$, which checks out: $15$ vertices, $14$ edges, degree sum $28 = 12 + 6 + 10$.

exam.prompt: A simple graph $G$ has $100$ vertices and $200$ edges. State (a) how many entries its adjacency matrix holds, (b) how many of those entries equal $1$, (c) the total number of neighbour entries across all its adjacency lists, and (d) the largest number of edges any simple graph on $100$ vertices could have. Justify each number briefly.
exam.explain: The matrix always holds $100^2 = 10000$ entries, of which $2 \times 200 = 400$ are $1$ because symmetry puts each edge on both sides of the diagonal, and the adjacency lists store exactly those $400$ endpoints and nothing else. The maximum is $\binom{100}{2} = 4950$, so $G$ uses about a twelfth of the possible edges - which is exactly the regime where lists beat matrices.

exam.prompt: An acyclic simple graph $F$ has $10$ vertices and $3$ connected components. How many edges does $F$ have? Explain why the answer follows from the tree edge count, and say what the answer would become if $F$ were connected instead.
exam.explain: Each component of an acyclic graph is connected and acyclic, hence a tree with $n_i - 1$ edges, and summing over the three components gives $\sum_i (n_i - 1) = 10 - 3 = 7$. Connected means $c = 1$, collapsing the formula back to $n - 1 = 9$ - so the components are precisely the edges a forest is missing relative to a tree.

exam.prompt: Let $G$ be a simple graph on $n$ vertices in which every vertex has degree at least $2$. Prove that $G$ contains a cycle. Argue by contradiction, using the handshake lemma together with the edge count of an acyclic graph.
exam.explain: Suppose $G$ were acyclic; it is then a forest with $c \geq 1$ components and exactly $n - c \leq n - 1$ edges. But the handshake lemma gives $2|E| = \sum_{v} \deg(v) \geq 2n$, so $|E| \geq n$, and $n \leq n - 1$ is false. The two facts pull in opposite directions - a minimum degree forces edges to exist, while acyclicity caps how many there can be.
